article_text:
Paris Photo and Aperture are pleased to announce the winners of the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards—an annual celebration of the vibrant field of photobook publishing. A final jury met in Paris on November 12 to select this year’s winners. The jury comprised Justine Kurland , photographer; Pablo Larios , writer and senior editor, Artforum ; Chiara Bardelli Nonino , features director, Harper’s Bazaar Italia ; Lou Stoppard , writer, critic, and curator; and Ferdinando Verderi , creative director.

“We were drawn to books that introduce a new approach within each of their respective categories, and that was a guiding principle in determining the final selections,” says juror Ferdinando Verderi. “Each of these four titles expands the creative possibilities of the medium, pushing photography in new directions and opening new conversations of what the photobook can be.”

This year, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world, including standout entries from Armenia, Iran, Morocco, Venezuela, and more. On September 22–24, the 2026 shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team: Alejandro Cartagena , artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron , director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti , editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas , artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma , curator and founder, Offset Projects.

A presentation of the thirty-five books shortlisted for the 2026 PhotoBook Awards, including the winners, is currently on view at Paris Photo through November 15 and will travel to Dublin at PhotoIreland, in December 2026, and other venues to be announced.

Below, read about this year’s winning titles.

Photography Catalog of the Year

L Is for Look: Children’s Photobooks , Edited by Anne Lacoste and Rose Durr Spector Books, Leipzig, Germany. Design by Ina Kwon and Helmut Völter

L Is for Look illuminates the vibrant but previously underexplored field of children’s photobooks. Featuring more than one hundred global examples, from the 1930s through the present, this catalog is organized thematically by editorial approach and concept: the pedagogical, designed to instruct toddlers on vocabulary or the alphabet or promote an understanding of geometric shapes and forms; fictional storytelling paired with photographs, creating tensions between invented narratives and depictions of reality; animals, often anthropomorphized and conversing; and “photographism,” the interaction of photography, graphic design, and other media. “This book is a thoroughly researched and visually compelling catalog documenting the intersection of photography and childhood,” says juror Chiara Bardelli Nonino, “from the emergence of image-based teaching methods to more experimental artistic endeavors.” The books assembled here no doubt captured the imaginations of young people when they were first published, just as this compendium, with its delightful array of visual pleasures—and rich contextual research—will be equally illuminating for readers of all ages today.

First PhotoBook

Notation(s) by Moeko Ishiguro Self-published, Tokyo. Design by Moeko Ishiguro

Moeko Ishiguro’s self-published debut feels less like a book than an intricate sculpture, dispensing as it does with traditional pagination in favor of folds, overlaps, and shifting layers that must be physically negotiated by the reader. The photographs—wryly observed and uncannily seductive shots of concrete planters, litter, and other mundane phenomena—are revealed through a process of peeling back layers of paper with notations, making each image appear discovered rather than simply turned to. Around the height and width of a smartphone, this book offers a brilliant alternative to passive scrolling, asking readers to spend time with images that refuse to surrender their core unknowability. “This book questions what it means to look and to see,” says Lou Stoppard. “It is a project that challenges the traditions of photobook-making and justifies itself as a book—it’s not a project that can be anything else.”

PhotoBook of the Year

Passports, 2012–2025 by Keisha Scarville MACK, London. Design by Keisha Scarville and Morgan Crowcroft-Brown

Since 2012, Keisha Scarville has been reworking an ID photo from her father’s first passport, taken when he was sixteen years old and living in Guyana. She has embellished each reproduction of the photo with daubs of paint or little beads or collaged images from magazines, amassing a collection of three hundred unique artworks. Sometimes her father has red skin; sometimes he’s surrounded by black stars. Tears of yellow ribbons fall from his eyes, or abstract masks obscure his face altogether. The tactile variations layered over the ID photo causes “an irrepressible urge to touch,” writes Tina M. Campt in Passports , a book that meditates on the love between a father and a daughter, and the ambiguous relationship between homeland and diaspora. “Scarville’s book explores how images hold histories, and how one can use photography to imagine a world they want to live in,” notes juror Justine Kurland. Scaled to the size of a novel and studded with ruminative lines from a dialogue with Scarville’s father, Passports , which gestures to the collages and painterly techniques of Lorna Simpson, Chris Ofili, and Kerry James Marshall, is an indelible photo-essay about the meaning of kinship.

Jurors’ Special Mention

Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences by Sara Bennett Kehrer Verlag, Heidelberg, Germany. Design by Teun van der Heijden and Heijdens Karwei

Following a career as a public defender, Sara Bennett spent over a decade photographing women convicted of violent crimes. Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences combines Bennett’s portraits of the women she met and collaborated with—spanning their lives inside prison walls to their reentry into the outside world—with personal ephemera like letters, polaroids, and drawings to weave a layered story of humanity. Each portrait is paired with a handwritten response to the question “When you see this photo . . . what does it make you think?” bearing witness to their experiences from within a cell to their reconciliation with feelings of regret and forgiveness. “The tenderness, poetry, and complexity of what Bennett documents, together with the degree of political commitment and personal devotion, reveals photography’s ability to move the dial on sociopolitical discussions,” says juror Pablo Larios. Shining a compassionate light on an often underrepresented population within the discourse surrounding mass incarceration, Bennett invites us to question the justice system as we know it.

An exhibition of 2026 PhotoBook Awards Shortlist will be on view at Paris Photo through November 15 and will travel to PhotoIreland, Dublin, in December 2026 and other venues to be announced.

"当然，在艾米莉·勃朗特的故事里，操尸体只是被暗示为逻辑上的下一步：一个角色挖开棺材，撕开一侧，然后躺在里面部分腐烂的尸体旁。所有这一切当然令人震惊，但它是带着无可否认的激情执行的。对我来说，这是衡量任何《呼啸山庄》改编作品的标准：它是否愿意成为勃朗特的同时代人但丁·加百列·罗塞蒂所说的“一个不可思议的怪物”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "芬内尔的怪物们——命途多舛的情侣凯茜（玛格罗比饰）和希刺克厉夫（雅各布·埃洛迪饰）——相比之下显得平淡无奇。除了大量泼洒深红色的疯狂布景设计外，很难让人看出这是执导过鲁莽而挑衅的《前程似锦的年轻女子》（2020）和《萨特本》（2023）的导演。也许是芬内尔试图攀登勃朗特这座大山，又或者，作为一名步入中年的千禧一代导演，她的锐气已经随着年龄消磨。或者是因为到了2026年，我们都太累了，所以我们得到了应得的《呼啸山庄》：一部软弱无力的作品。电影改编自故事的前半部分，年轻的希刺克厉夫被厄恩肖先生（马丁·克鲁尼斯饰）带到荒凉的西约克郡荒原上的家族庄园——呼啸山庄。故事讲述了这个男孩与厄恩肖的女儿凯茜之间建立的羁绊，先是作为孩子，然后是成年人。经过一系列误解，凯茜嫁给了富有的埃德加·兰顿（沙扎德·拉蒂夫饰），而为了气她，希刺克厉夫娶了兰顿的监护对象伊莎贝拉（艾莉森·奥利弗饰）。（在小说中她是他的妹妹。）凯茜的身体逐渐虚弱并死去，表面上是因为心碎，在她死后，希刺克厉夫要求她作为鬼魂回来，永远折磨他。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "芬内尔的版本被大大删减了。她舍弃了关键角色，包括凯茜的哥哥欣德利，他对希刺克厉夫早期的虐待激发了后者终身的复仇行动，并且她还改动了重要的细节，比如希刺克厉夫模糊的种族身份。在这部电影中，他没有被叫作“吉普赛人”；周围没有欣德利来吐出这个词。相反，欣德利的敌意被分摊到了两个角色身上：厄恩肖先生（现在成了一个俗套的虐待狂父亲）和娜莉（洪秀饰，原著中厄恩肖家的仆人），她密谋让凯茜和希刺克厉夫分开。她的阶级得到了提升，成了一名伴侣，如果不是因为她私生子的出身（显然生父/生母是亚洲人？我分不清选角是无视种族还是纯粹为了装饰），她本可以成为一位女士。希刺克厉夫仇恨的根源几乎消失殆尽，他和凯茜关系的利害关系也随之消失。与书中传达的那种命中注定无法在一起的宿命感不同，他们的结合是被愚蠢的人为设计所阻挠的。", article_text:
I’m going to start with a spoiler, because we’re talking about a nearly 200-year-old novel with more than a dozen film adaptations: there is no corpse-fucking in Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights .

Granted, in Emily Brontë’s story, the corpse-fucking is only implied as the logical next step after a character digs up a coffin, rips open one side, and lies with the partially decayed body inside. All of this is of course shocking, but it is carried out with undeniable passion. For me, this is the measure of any Wuthering Heights adaptation: its willingness to become what Brontë contemporary Dante Gabriel Rossetti called “an incredible monster.”

Fennell’s monsters—the doomed lovers Cathy (Margot Robbie) and Heathcliff (Jacob Elordi)—are comparatively vanilla. And besides the bonkers set design, amply splashed with crimson, it’s hard to recognize the director of the brash and provocative Promising Young Woman (2020) and Saltburn (2023). Maybe it’s the Brontë mountain Fennell’s trying to climb, or maybe, as a millennial director settling into middle age, she’s aged out of her edge. Or maybe, because it’s 2026, and we are all so very tired, it’s that we are getting the Wuthering Heights we deserve: a limp one. The film adapts the first half of the story, in which a young Heathcliff is brought by Mr. Earnshaw (Martin Clunes) to Wuthering Heights, the family estate on the barren West Yorkshire Moors. It follows the bond that develops between the boy and Earnshaw’s daughter Cathy, first as children, then as adults. After a series of misunderstandings, Cathy marries the rich Edgar Linton (Shazad Latif), and to spite her, Heathcliff weds Isabella (Alison Oliver), Linton’s ward. (She is his sister in the novel.) Cathy gradually weakens and dies, ostensibly of a broken heart, and upon her death Heathcliff demands that she return as a ghost, forever to torment him.

Fennell’s version is significantly pared down. She sheds key characters, including Cathy’s brother Hindley, whose early cruelty to Heathcliff inspires his lifelong campaign of vengeance, and alters important details, like Heathcliff’s ethnic ambiguity. In this film, he is not called a “gipsy”; there’s no Hindley around to say the word. Hindley’s antagonism is instead divided between two characters: Mr. Earnshaw, now a generically abusive dad, and Nelly (Hong Chau), the Earnshaws’ servant in the book, who schemes to keep Cathy and Heathcliff apart. She gets a class upgrade to companion, and she would be a lady were it not for her illegitimate birth (apparently by an Asian parent? I can’t tell whether the casting is blind to race or uses it decoratively). The source of Heathcliff’s animus has all but disappeared, and so too have the stakes of his relationship with Cathy. Instead of its fated impossibility, as it is conveyed in the book, their union is impeded by silly contrivances.

Brontë’s Cathy and Heathcliff are like forces of nature. Both are described as “wild”: Cathy, “a wild, hatless little savage,” and Heathcliff, “an unreclaimed creature, without refinement, without cultivation; an arid wilderness of furze and whinstone.” They cannot be controlled, even by their own selves. Fennell gives us toy versions. Her Heathcliff patiently takes lashings from Mr. Earnshaw and waits out Cathy’s bouts of temper. Despite Elordi’s hard abs, visible underneath a persistently rain-soaked shirt, his Heathcliff is strangely soft. Cathy, meanwhile, may be spirited and sharp-eyed, but she never really outgrows her girlishness. She’s understandably attracted to Heathcliff after he returns from a prolonged absence—who wouldn’t be, especially now that he’s sporting an earring and a gold tooth? But is it a matter of amour fou, or the marital boredom Cathy complained of in the previous scene?

Surely Fennell has the right to make her own version of the novel—that’s what the quotation marks that adorn the film’s official title are for. But that doesn’t mean she has crafted a good film, even on its own terms. The problem with a “reimagining” of this sort is not too little source material, but too much of it. The excisions and substitutions throw the work off-balance. Scrubbed elements leave a residue, while remaining ones totter in the absence of their previous supports. Nelly is mad about something, but it’s never clear what she’s after. When Heathcliff first arrives, she seems jealous, but why? Later, after Cathy upbraids her with a stinging remark, she prompts Cathy to admit that marrying Heathcliff would “degrade” her, knowing all the while that Heathcliff is listening on the other side of the door. In the novel, this pivotal scene is described by Nelly herself, the book’s narrator. If she acted maliciously, she did not do so consciously. Here, her snap retaliation is just petty.

Fennell offers no motivation for Nelly’s behavior, or really that of any character besides Cathy and Heathcliff. Those two love each other, and are horny for each other, which is reason enough to keep the story going, though when and how those feelings bloomed are left unexplained. Everyone else is just set dressing, there only to move forward or stall the central relationship. This is a shame, because Fennell’s most interesting character is Isabella. In the novel, she is the innocent victim of Cathy and Heathcliff’s sick games, but here she is granted a surprising sturdiness. Her eccentricities are played for laughs, but she relishes everything she does. She loves ribbons—she has an entire room dedicated to ribbons!—and naughty découpage. She makes creepy little dolls with bits of Cathy’s hair, then stages them in an enormous dollhouse, an exact replica of the Lintons’ home. (Their mansion’s hallucinatory décor, a mix of Hollywood Regency and what could be called “putrid fairy tale,” seems also to have come straight from Isabella’s imagination.) When Heathcliff bursts through her window with a loveless offer of marriage, she obliges with full consent. This is the kinkiest moment in the film—and certainly sexier than the steamy bodice-ripping promised in the film’s promotional materials. In the shadow of Heathcliff’s tortured relationship with Cathy, he forges one with Isabella that, despite or perhaps because of its depravity, is honest.

To her credit, Fennell understands that it’s more fun to smash a dollhouse than to construct one meticulously. Her sledgehammer approach to party scenes in her previous films is rivaled by Wuthering Heights ’s opening sequence of a public hanging. Though we are supposed to be in the late 18th century, the mood is more medieval. After a few moments of the hanged man’s dying gasps, a Charli xcx song floods the soundtrack (the truly terrifying track “House,” which she recorded with John Cale), and the crowd erupts in a carnal frenzy. People roar, some start fucking, a nun closes her eyes, and parents pull away their children. The scene does not exist in Brontë’s novel, but it’s somehow closest to the monstrous vitality of that world, a place where the dead refuse to die. Too bad that Fennell never gives her characters the chance to live.

article_text:
[Editor’s note: The following article contains spoilers for “ You Can See Everything .”]

If cinematographer David Bolen and camera operator Jonathan Mitchell were filming verité coverage of the IndieWire office in New York after the release of Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder ‘s “You Can See Everything,” there would have been a similar visual sense of transience — a latent, unsettling tension of the kind that characterizes the first half of the A24 film , where Oppenheim, Fielder, and their small team were documenting Elizabeth Holmes’ last month of freedom before reporting to prison to serve her sentence for multiple counts of fraud.

Mostly, this was because we’re moving to a different floor of the office, and there were a lot of cardboard boxes, abandoned Tupperware, and mystery mugs scattered about. But it was also because of the impact of “You Can See Everything” — our individual reactions to it on staff and the wider reactions that we were seeing around the Internet.

The latter led our stalwart TV Critic, Ben Travers, to pose a question: Given the weekend that Fielder just had with “You Can See Everything,” would the filmmaker be more or less keen on a third season of “The Rehearsal,” his HBO series which has allowed him to do everything from bring the recreation of a Brooklyn bar across state lines to fly a commercial airliner?

I, Craft Editor Sarah Shachat, will admit that I wasn’t thinking too rigorously when I said the words, “He’s already made Season 3. It’s this movie,” but they were out before I thought to stop them. And look, we know from HBO Head of Comedy Casey Bloys that “ The Rehearsal ” Season 3 is in the works. Reddit is already trying to sleuth out whether Nathan Fielder intends to release the Epstein files or successfully transit the Strait of Hormuz, or whatever he’s planning on doing; IndieWire doesn’t know any more than you do.

But certain aspects of “You Can See Everything” do take on a distinct light when considered in the shadow of what Fielder (and Oppenheim) have done before. There are also a number of ways in which it is the Pokémon evolution of their previous work — and in which specifically “The Rehearsal” prepared, if not Fielder himself, than his audience to roll with a self-reflexiveness so recursive that even Peter Watkins would be like, “Wait, they did what?”

One of the core draws of the first season of “The Rehearsal” was its intricate sets — the great Nate’s Lizard Lounge, of course, but also studio builds of apartments. and locations thoroughly dressed by the show’s art team. “The Rehearsal” teaches us how to see that everything we interact with is constructed. Spaces aren’t ever just real or fake. If they’re real, they’re recreated and repurposed, often more than once while Fielder and his laptop loom in the center. If they’re “faked” for the show, they’re often where the most interesting and emotional exploration among the participants takes place.

Contrast Kor’s introduction in Episode 1 of the show with Angela’s in Episode 2. We first see Kor in his actual home, and while it’s safe to assume that the scene of the New York teacher playing along with “Jeopardy!” was staged for the cameras, there’s still a sense that we’re observing his day-to-day reality. With Angela, we start mid-rehearsal, first with a wall of surveillance cameras that pulls back to reveal Fielder in the control room/video village alongside the production crew and two mothers of children who’ll be playing Angela’s faux son, Adam. We see the artifice first, the person second. That colors how we move through both stories and understand those people, and Fielder’s relationship with them.

The first season of “The Rehearsal” questions what kind of authenticity can come out of an artificial setup or environment, especially for folks who have trouble expressing themselves. Maybe the artifice of “rehearsing” can lead to something good and genuine. The season becomes deeply concerned with the blurring of true emotion and performance — and how, for good and for ill, it’s much harder to draw a line between those things than it might seem. The question becomes even more fraught when it comes to child actors, where adults have a duty of care to try and keep reality straight for them while putting them in a situation where it starts to bend.

Here’s where the spoilers start — so seriously, don’t read unless you’ve already seen “You Can See Everything.”

When the “You Can See Everything” returns to the rental home in San Diego where Elizabeth Holmes and her boyfriend Billy Evans spent their last few months before moving down to Texas to comply with Holmes’ prison sentence, Nathan Fielder and Amanda Seyfried are looking for a grounding in the details of the space Holmes is no longer in, obviously. They’re also looking to bend reality far enough into artifice that they may actually be able to come back around to some truth. If Fielder and Oppenheim can run back the baffling month they spent in Del Mar through the scenes with Seyfried (as well as a game Christopher Abbott), maybe they can finally understand it, and Holmes.

There’s still some of those nearly invisible touches to it, though. Seyfried finds the now infamous bowl for beating eggs in the cabinet where it’s been the whole time, but when the film cuts to the recreation of Seyfried-as-Holmes and Fielder (as himself) meeting for the first time, a set decoration team has made the house look lived-in again. The rhythmic back-and-forth between the script that Fielder and Seyfried perform and the two of them discussing that scene as Fielder’s memory of a real event, is also an intentional grounding of how we interpret what we’re seeing.

That first recreation starts with Fielder and Seyfried’s conversation, cuts to the recreation itself, and continues with Fielder talking to Seyfried in a makeup chair, getting dressed for the role. The verite footage, conversation within a staged setting, and full recreation all exist on a spectrum of reality, one that “You Can See Everything” is very careful to guide us through with the goal of helping us come to some conclusion (or grapple with our inability to draw one). It’s similar arc just in that one sequence to the full first season of “The Rehearsal.”

In other words, Nathan and editor Adam Locke-Norton learned it from watching Nathan.

They learned even more from Season 2 of “The Rehearsal,” which grapples with the struggle for any one of us to be able to successfully communicate to another person, even when the stakes are life and death. The first episode of Season 2 goes into this in depth, but one only needs to watch the painful interview CNN did with Fielder about the show to see how easy it is for people to dismiss anything said by a comedian, even some extremely salient points about the safety that rides on good communication between pilots in the cockpit, and how it is in desperate need of improvement.

Beyond that dilemma, the extent to which any of us can successfully understand each other is at issue in both “You Can See Everything” and “The Rehearsal” Season 2. The HBO show does a fantastic job of exploring the pressures and incentives, implicit and explicit, that prevent pilots from communicating better. The recreations in Season 2, be they of a fully functional airport terminal or Fielder embodying Sully Sullenberg for “the miracle on the Hudson” after speed-running thorugh playing the pilot’s entire life, are in service of explicating and exploring those communication hangups — with cheeky a little bit of Evanessance thrown in, too.

The recreations in “You Can See Everything” are about trying to create a fuller picture of imperfect communication to fully understand the extent to which it’s genuine or not. It is a fascinating inverse of Season 2 of “The Rehearsal,” where Fielder actually becomes a pilot rated to fly a 737 and does so, on camera, carrying the entire extended cast of actors that have participated in Season 2 for the finale of the season. Fielder becomes his subject not just within the frame of the show itself, but in his lived experience, and that transformation has an impact on how he thinks about himself.

Grappling with the potential of seeing Holmes in prison but not being able to film or record the conversation in any way, Fielder talks it through with Seyfried. The actor is willing to recreate whatever Fielder needs. But Fielder isn’t sure that even she can be fully accurate — that her performance really can give us a chance to judge what Holmes has to say.

Of course they do end up shooting the recreation, intercut with Fielder and Seyfried talking through the script he’s written up before a fireplace that’s lit so dramatically Hitchcock wishes he put it in “Vertigo.” But there are conscious choices made here beyond the choice to do it. The first section of the sequence, where Fielder arrives at the prison and waits in the visiting room for a long time before Holmes shows up, unfolds with normal coverage — wides, medium wides on Fielder, insert shots of the vending machines, and so on. When Seyfried-as-Holmes does enter the scene, she’s covered from the back, in wides, and we’re unable to see Seyfried’s face.

There is a corner of the multiverse where Oppenheim and Fielder stage the entire conversation between Fielder and Holmes that way. The filmmakers could’ve let key moments of what Holmes says fall on Seyfried-as-herself, reading the script, and let whatever “true” version of Holmes — her expressions, her bearing her chemistry with Fielder — there is to be had all live inside the audience’s mind. There is a version of this sequence that withholds Seyfried’s interpretation in the name of “truth.”

Instead, we see Seyfried give a performance that we can never know is fully accurate; but in moments where she says, as Holmes “I’m tired of having other people speak for me” sure feels true. It feels lived . “You Can See Everything” is the opposite of Season 2 of “The Rehearsal” as well as its cautionary escalation. The film shows how natural it can be to get lost inside of a transformative performance, and that however close to accuracy we can get, it is never close enough.

It is Seyfried herself, arguably the true heroine of the film, who points out that the more time Fielder has spent with Holmes, the trickier it may be for him not to care about her, and for their relationship not to color what we see.

But as both “The Rehearsal” and “You Can See Everything” point out, time with each other is all we have.

“You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters.

article_text:
Der Filmkritiker Lukas Stern hat den Siegfried Kracauer Preis 2026 gewonnen. Seine Rezension zu „Vier minus drei“ wurde im Rahmen der Kinoprogrammpreis-Gala in Köln als beste Filmkritik ausgezeichnet. Der Preis für die beste innovative Form ging an Max Osenstätter, Klaus Uhrig, Judith Goetsch und Johannes Munzinger für ihren Podcast „Werner Herzog – zu groß für Deutschland“.

Der Filmkritiker Lukas Stern ist der Gewinner des mit 5.000 Euro dotierten Siegfried Kracauer Preis 2026 in der Kategorie Beste Filmkritik. Die Jury zeichnete seine Rezension zu dem Film „ Vier minus drei " von Adrian Goiginger aus. Der ebenfalls mit 5.000 Euro dotierte Preis in der Kategorie Beste innovative Form der Filmkritik ging an das Team Max Osenstätter, Klaus Uhrig, Judith Goetsch und Johannes Munzinger für ihren sechsteiligen Podcast „Werner Herzog – zu groß für Deutschland“ . Die feierliche Verleihung fand im Rahmen des Kinoprogrammpreis NRW in der Wolkenburg in Köln statt.

„Das erste Wort, der erste Satz: Wie finde ich den passenden Einstieg, wie den Schluss? Welches Gegengewicht setze ich dem Schmerz entgegen, einer schier unerträglichen, sinnlosen Trostlosigkeit, um ein Publikum zu gewinnen, ohne es zu verlieren?“, schreibt die Jury über die Auszeichnung der Filmkritik von Lukas Stern und lobt insbesondere die Herausforderung des Textes: „Sprachwitz und Scharfsinn waren schon immer gute Ratgeber. Glücklicherweise findet diese Kritik ihre Antworten im Film selbst. Erst im schmerzhaften Abschied von den anderen erkennen wir den unendlichen Wert des Lebens.“ Die Kritik zum Film „Vier minus drei“ bringt diese Erkenntnis unverblümt auf den Punkt: „Dem Publikum steht eine emotionale Grenzerfahrung bevor, ein körperlicher Kontrollverlust. Einerseits. Und doch setzt der Text immer wieder Anker der Hoffnung. Der Lebenswille wird so eindringlich spürbar, dass am Ende die Neugier überwiegt. Sprachwitz und Scharfsinn waren schon immer gute Ratgeber“.

In der Kategorie Beste innovative Form der Filmkritik zeichnete die Jury Max Osenstätter, Klaus Uhrig, Judith Goetsch und Johannes Munzinger für den Podcast „ Werner Herzog – zu groß für Deutschland “ aus. „Wer ist der Mensch, der auf YouTube von Klaus Kinski angeschrien wird?“, fragt sich der „hochwertig produzierte Podcast. Auch wenn oder gerade weil Werner Herzog zu keiner Zusammenarbeit bereit war, entstand ein gut recherchierter, unterhaltsamer Podcast – nicht zuletzt dank einiger Interviews mit WegbegleiterInnen des Regisseurs.“ Die sechs Folgen à vierzig Minuten richten sich an ein jüngeres Publikum, dem Herzogs Person und Werk nahegebracht werden sollen. „Der Podcast zeugt nicht nur von einer tiefen Auseinandersetzung mit seinem Gegenstand, sondern findet dafür außerdem eine durchweg spannende und abwechslungsreiche Erzählweise“, so die Jury.

Die Preise wurden von Filmemacher Tom Tykwer übergeben, der bei der Verleihung auch von seinem eigenen Verhältnis zur Filmkritik erzählte. Das ist eine durchaus nicht unkomplizierte Angelegenheit, da ihn manche Wortmeldungen durchaus verzweifeln ließen, andere ihn aber auch regelrecht beglückt haben. Denn es gibt „immer wieder Stimmen, die einen daran erinnern, was das für eine Kunst ist“.

Die nach dem Filmtheoretiker Siegfried Kracauer benannte Auszeichnung wird jährlich vergeben. Zur dreiköpfigen Jury aus den Sparten Festival, Kino und Kritik gehörten die Kinoleiterin Ulrike Schüler (Bambi Kino Gütersloh), der Festivalleiter Gregor Maria Schubert sowie die Kritikerin Rahel Jung.

Der Siegfried Kracauer Preis ist eine gemeinsame Initiative der MFG Filmförderung Baden-Württemberg (MFG), der Film- und Medienstiftung NRW und der Hessen Film & Medien in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Verband der deutschen Filmkritik (VdFk). Die Auslober würdigen damit die Filmkritik als einen wichtigen Faktor für den langfristigen Bestand und die Weiterentwicklung einer vielfältigen Kinokultur.

article_text:
Jusqu’au 7 novembre, la commune de Fontenay-sous-Bois accueille la première édition de FLASH, festival social et citoyen qui dresse un portrait des périphéries, urbaines, sociales ou intimes, à travers des images d’archives et contemporaines. Plusieurs artistes ont été invité·es à explorer cette thématique, notamment Carolina Arantes , Léa Rivera-Hadjes ou encore Mohamed Bourouissa , qui présente son film documentaire expérimental Noubia .

Fontenay-sous-Bois a cette particularité de se raconter à travers sa topographie. Construite sur deux versants, la commune juxtapose des réalités sociales qui se côtoient sans toujours se rencontrer : d’un côté, des quartiers plus aisés tournés vers Paris et le bois de Vincennes ; de l’autre, autour de Val-de-Fontenay, des ensembles sortis de terre entre les années 1950 et 1970.

C’est précisément ce désir de créer du lien entre les différentes composantes de la ville qui est au cœur de FLASH. Pour sa première édition, le festival s’est installé à la Halle Roublot, ancien marché couvert transformé en pôle artistique. Un lieu où Émilie Chazelle et Margaux Hannart ont imaginé un projet qui dépasse le seul cadre de l’exposition pour faire de la photographie un catalyseur de rencontres, de transmission et de mise en relation : « FLASH est avant tout un festival social et citoyen, qui utilise le médium photographique comme outil d ’interrogation et de valorisation des territoires et populations périphériques. »

Une périphérie envisagée au-delà de sa dimension géographique

Toutes deux ont grandi autour de Cergy-Pontoise, dans une banlieue dont elles retiennent autant la richesse de la mixité sociale et culturelle que le manque de représentation. Avec FLASH, elles entendent déplacer le regard vers ces territoires, leurs habitant·es et leurs histoires à travers trois volets : une exposition réunissant des artistes contemporain·es dont les œuvres explorent cette idée de marge ; un volet plus historique imaginé à partir d’archives photographiques liées à Fontenay-sous-Bois ; et enfin un troisième, essentiellement participatif, issu d’un travail collaboratif avec la population locale.

Au cœur de FLASH, Émilie Chazelle et Margaux Hannart placent une conception élargie de la périphérie, envisagée au-delà de sa seule dimension géographique, dans ses aspects sociaux ou intimes : « Il y a notamment ce sentiment d’être à la marge de la société, d ’une communauté, voire de soi-mê me. » Pour elles, l’intime est résolument politique.

C’est ce qu’illustre l’exposition Trajectoire(s) , qui réunit douze artistes contemporain·es explorant les différentes formes de marginalité à travers la photographie, le film, la sculpture, le livre ou l’installation. Plusieurs projets sont consacrés à la jeunesse et à la quête de soi. Avec La Vie immé diate , Sandra Rocha livre ainsi un journal intime collectif dans lequel des adolescent·es livrent leur perception de l’avenir. Leurs mots dialoguent avec des clichés transfigurés par des jeux de collage. Plus loin, dans des images en noir et blanc où affleure une poésie toute en retenue, Gil Lesage documente la transition de genre de son enfant.

D’autres séries, comme celle d’Anne Mocaër, s’intéressent à la manière dont les transformations urbaines affectent celles et ceux qui habitent la ville. Avec Avenue Royale , la photographe donne un visage aux habitant·es d’un quartier de Casablanca pris depuis plus de trente ans dans un vaste projet de réaménagement, entre démolitions annoncées et promesses de relogement. Hicham Gardaf et Rio Saito observent quant à eux des formes de vie façonnées par la ville et ses mutations : le premier filme à Tanger les vendeurs de Javel, métier voué à disparaître face à l’urbanisation accélérée ; le second s’intéresse aux habitant·es de la périphérie du Caire qui traversent chaque jour le Ring Road au péril de leur vie pour rejoindre le centre-ville. Les trajectoires féminines et les questions d’émancipation traversent également les travaux de Mohamed Bourouissa, Sabrina Belouaar ou encore Laïs Decaster. Cette dernière prend pour décor le Car Wash , une station de lavage où sa sœur, tout en nettoyant sa voiture, raconte le rapport d’indépendance, de séduction et de liberté qu’elle entretient avec celle-ci.

Plus loin, les expositions Fragments d ’une histoire collective et Banlieue en fête ! racontent Fontenay-sous-Bois à travers ses célébrations collectives pour la première, qui puise dans les archives municipales de la commune, et intimes pour la seconde, imaginée à partir des clichés personnels des Fontenaisien·nes. Une exposition qui cristallise l’ambition du festival de devenir une plateforme collaborative et participative. Les nombreux partenariats et ateliers organisés autour de FLASH prolongent cette volonté. Si le festival a été pensé comme une biennale, les ateliers se poursuivront tout au long de l’année afin de maintenir un lien avec la population locale. À terme, FLASH ambitionne de se développer et d’investir d’autres lieux de la ville. De quoi, surtout, inscrire durablement la photographie dans un territoire où elle était jusqu’ici peu présente.

title_original: Art Market: Flora Yukhnovich, Portia Zvavahera e Ben Sledsens tra i protagonisti di ottobre
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Torna l’appuntamento mensile con gli artisti che hanno animato il segmento ultra-contemporaneo nelle ultime settimane. 383 sono i lotti analizzati a ottobre, con un sell-through rate del 79% e un fatturato complessivo di $19.726.465. Sei le case d’asta prese in esame: Bonhams, China Guardian, Christie’s, Phillips, Poly Auction e Sotheby’s. E non sono mancati i record: da Joseph Yaeger , già protagonista della nostra analisi di maggio, a Portia Zvavahera, passando per Megan Rooney, Maarten Baas ed Eva Helene Pade.", "links": [{"text": "analisi di maggio,", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/mercato/art-market-joseph-yaeger-ding-shilun-e-salman-toor-tra-i-giovani-protagonisti-di-maggio/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tre sono gli artisti selezionati questo mese a cui corrispondono risultati che restituiscono differenti indicatori di tenuta del mercato: la capacità di Flora Yukhnovich (1990) di confermare quotazioni elevate, mantenendosi in prossimità del proprio record; la continuità di Ben Sledsens (1991), sostenuta da tre aggiudicazioni e da un andamento complessivamente superiore alle aspettative; infine, l’exploit di Portia Zvavahera (1985), il cui nuovo record testimonia una significativa accelerazione della domanda. Tra conferme e nuove performance, ottobre offre così tre diverse chiavi di lettura del segmento ultra-contemporaneo."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Flora Yukhnovich (1990)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Durante l’asta del 14 ottobre 20th/21st Century: London Evening Sale d a Christie’s, l’opera Capriccio , 2019, con una stima iniziale tra 1 e 1,5 milioni di sterline, è stata venduta per £2.286.000 ($3.017.520), il 52% sopra la stima massima. Questo risultato di poco si discosta dal suo record di £2.697.000 ($3.596.623) del 2022 con la vendita dell’opera Warm, Wet N’ Wild, 2020 da Sotheby’s. L’artista britannica Flora Yukhnovich ha studiato alla Guilds of London Art School e alla Heatherley School of Fine Art, e ha conseguito un Foundation in Art and Design alla Kingston University di Londra. Le sue opere fluttuano tra astrazione e figurativismo ispirandosi al Rococò e al Barocco, a nature morte olandesi del XVII secolo e all’espressionismo astratto che intreccia con la mitologia, la letteratura, il cinema e alla cultura dei consumi. La sua ultima mostra personale istituzionale si è tenuta nel 2025 alla Frick Collection con il titolo “Flora Yukhnovich’s Four Seasons” a New York. Rappresentata dalle gallerie Victoria Miro e Hauser & Wirth, quest’ultima ha presentato nel mese di ottobre, a Frieze London 2026 nella sezione Frieze Masters, un nuovo dipinto, realizzato ed esposto in risposta diretta accanto al capolavoro del pittore Jan Brueghel il Vecchio. article_text:
Torna l’appuntamento mensile con gli artisti che hanno animato il segmento ultra-contemporaneo nelle ultime settimane. 383 sono i lotti analizzati a ottobre, con un sell-through rate del 79% e un fatturato complessivo di $19.726.465. Sei le case d’asta prese in esame: Bonhams, China Guardian, Christie’s, Phillips, Poly Auction e Sotheby’s. E non sono mancati i record: da Joseph Yaeger , già protagonista della nostra analisi di maggio, a Portia Zvavahera, passando per Megan Rooney, Maarten Baas ed Eva Helene Pade.

Tre sono gli artisti selezionati questo mese a cui corrispondono risultati che restituiscono differenti indicatori di tenuta del mercato: la capacità di Flora Yukhnovich (1990) di confermare quotazioni elevate, mantenendosi in prossimità del proprio record; la continuità di Ben Sledsens (1991), sostenuta da tre aggiudicazioni e da un andamento complessivamente superiore alle aspettative; infine, l’exploit di Portia Zvavahera (1985), il cui nuovo record testimonia una significativa accelerazione della domanda. Tra conferme e nuove performance, ottobre offre così tre diverse chiavi di lettura del segmento ultra-contemporaneo.

Flora Yukhnovich (1990)

Durante l’asta del 14 ottobre 20th/21st Century: London Evening Sale d a Christie’s, l’opera Capriccio , 2019, con una stima iniziale tra 1 e 1,5 milioni di sterline, è stata venduta per £2.286.000 ($3.017.520), il 52% sopra la stima massima. Questo risultato di poco si discosta dal suo record di £2.697.000 ($3.596.623) del 2022 con la vendita dell’opera Warm, Wet N’ Wild, 2020 da Sotheby’s. L’artista britannica Flora Yukhnovich ha studiato alla Guilds of London Art School e alla Heatherley School of Fine Art, e ha conseguito un Foundation in Art and Design alla Kingston University di Londra. Le sue opere fluttuano tra astrazione e figurativismo ispirandosi al Rococò e al Barocco, a nature morte olandesi del XVII secolo e all’espressionismo astratto che intreccia con la mitologia, la letteratura, il cinema e alla cultura dei consumi. La sua ultima mostra personale istituzionale si è tenuta nel 2025 alla Frick Collection con il titolo “Flora Yukhnovich’s Four Seasons” a New York. Rappresentata dalle gallerie Victoria Miro e Hauser & Wirth, quest’ultima ha presentato nel mese di ottobre, a Frieze London 2026 nella sezione Frieze Masters, un nuovo dipinto, realizzato ed esposto in risposta diretta accanto al capolavoro del pittore Jan Brueghel il Vecchio. Le sue opere sono presenti in importanti collezioni pubbliche, tra cui il Brooklyn Museum, Government Art Collection in Inghilterra e Montreal Museum of Fine Arts.

Ben Sledsens (1991)

L’artista belga Ben Sledsens ha registrato nel mese di ottobre 2026 un fatturato aggregato di $983.448 con la vendita di tre opere e una media del 60% sopra la stima. Il risultato più interessante è stato ottenuto da Phillips, durante la Modern & Contemporary Art Evening Sale di Londra del 15 ottobre, con la vendita dell’opera Between Trees, 2023-2024 per £387.000 con un + 94%. Sledsens , in asta dal 2021, ha raggiunto il suo record di £504.000 nel 2023 con la vendita dell’opera Throwing Dice , 2016 da Christie’s, durante l’asta Post-War and Contemporary Art Day Sale. L’artista trae ispirazione, per le sue opere ricche di natura, da Rousseau, Matisse e Bonnard. Nel 2022 si è tenuta la mostra personale Ben Sledsens al CAC Malaga (Centro de Arte Contemporáneo de Málaga). Nel 2026 ha partecipato alla mostra collettiva Finding Neverland alla Nassima Foundation di Tel Aviv. Rappresentato da Tim Van Laere Gallery, ad Art Basel Paris 2026 ha registrato una vendita da $190.000. È presente in diverse collezioni pubbliche, tra cui: il Centraal Museum Utrecht, l’M HKA (Museum of Contemporary Art Antwerp) e il Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego.

Portia Zvavahera (1985)

Durante l’asta Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection Evening Sale da Christie’s a Londra, il 14 ottobre, l’opera This is where I travelled [3], 2020, con una stima iniziale tra £70.000 e £100.000, è stata venduta per £307.200, il 207% sopra la stima massima, stabilendo così il suo nuovo record. L’artista zimbabwese, che ha fatto il suo ingresso in asta nel 2020, utilizza complesse tecniche di stampa e pennellate energiche per dare forma a composizioni che si ispirano alle tradizioni figurative della sua terra. Ha studiato presso il BAT Visual Arts Studio, National Gallery of Zimbabwe e presso l’Harare Polytechnic, dove ha conseguito un diploma in belle arti. Ha partecipato alla Biennale di Venezia sia nel 2013 sia nel 2022. La prima mostra istituzionale negli Stati Uniti è stata inaugurata nel 2025 presso l’Institute of Contemporary Art di Boston con il titolo Hidden Battles / Hondo dzakavanzika. È rappresentata da David Zwirner e da Stevenson, che l’hanno portata a Frieze London 2026, Zwirner ha registrato la vendita di un suo nuovo dipinto per $300.000. Ha preso parte ad Art Basel Paris nella sezione Oh La La! È presente in diverse collezioni pubbliche, tra cui la Johannesburg Art Gallery, il Pérez Art Museum Miami e la Tate di Londra.

article_text:
On Tuesday, the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) returned 22 antiquities to Greece . The cache includes decorated pottery from the 8th through the 4th centuries BCE that had been seized during an illegal antiquities trafficking investigation in and around Tel Aviv in 2020.

The ceremony took place at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens and was attended by Lina Mendoni, the Greek Minister of Culture; Pninat Yanai, the Israeli Ambassador to Greece; and Amir Ganor, director of the IAA’s Anti Theft Prevention Unit. This handover marks the first time Israel has returned contested items to Greece.

In a social media post , the IAA states that the 2020 seizure involved raids of an unnamed gallery, warehouses, and apartments which uncovered “thousands of archaeological items from Israel and around the world.” The investigation was prompted by suspicion of looting at ancient sites in the Mediterranean. The IAA does not clarify why it took Israel six years to return the items to Greece, or if objects belonging to other nations are also in the process of being repatriated. It is also not clear from where in Greece the items were looted.

Among the items back on Greek soil are black- and red-figure vessels, some with handles, decorated with scenes from Greek mythology, and would have been used in everyday life or as burial offerings. Among the vases of varying shapes and sizes (15 Attic vessels and six Corinthian, according to the Jerusalem Post ) was a bronze female figure.

Lina Mendoni, the Greek Minister of Culture, said that “this return lays the foundation for deepening cooperation between our countries in the field of protecting cultural heritage. Every return of antiquities to their country of origin also carries with it a broad moral and symbolic significance.”

She added that the return, “reminds us all that protecting cultural heritage is a shared responsibility, and that the effective fight against the illegal trade in antiquities requires cooperation between countries, mutual trust, and a commitment to upholding the law and strengthening heritage.”

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "本周的播客节目中，《Film Comment》编辑德维卡·吉里什（Devika Girish）和克林顿·克鲁特（Clinton Krute）采访了编剧兼导演诺亚·鲍姆巴赫（Noah Baumbach），他的新片《杰·凯利》目前正在部分影院上映。影片由乔治·克鲁尼（George Clooney）主演，饰演一位步入晚年的好莱坞明星，正面对他通往巅峰之路所做出的种种选择。剧情围绕杰前往托斯卡纳参加一项向其职业生涯致敬的活动展开，随行的还有由亚当·桑德勒（Adam Sandler）、劳拉·邓恩（Laura Dern）等人饰演的经纪团队，而他作为朋友、爱人和父母时所犯下的错则如影随形地困扰着他。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《杰·凯利》融合了费里尼风格的记忆剧场、受疯喜剧启发的火车之旅，以及对电影制作世界的自我反思性沉思，最终抵达某种具有普遍意义的内核；正如诺亚在我们的对话中所说，影片核心的主题一直是激励他许多作品创作的动力：如何与无法挽回的过去达成妥协。我们还讨论了他出色的演员阵容选择，他和剧组如何搭建布景以呈现如梦似幻的记忆片段（未使用CGI特效），以及更多内容。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
This week on the podcast, Film Comment Editors Devika Girish and Clinton Krute spoke to writer-director Noah Baumbach, whose new feature, Jay Kelly , is in select theaters now. The movie stars George Clooney as an aging Hollywood star reckoning with the choices he’s made on his way to the top. The action unfolds on a trip Jay takes to a tribute to his career in Tuscany, trailed by an entourage of handlers played by Adam Sandler, Laura Dern, and others, and haunted by his missteps as a friend, lover, and parent.

Jay Kelly blends Fellini-esque memory theater, a screwball-inspired train journey, and a self-reflexive contemplation on the world of filmmaking to arrive at something universal; as Noah says in our conversation, the theme at the heart of the film is one that has animated many of his works: coming to terms with an irretrievable past. We also talked about his remarkable casting choices, how he and his crew built sets to facilitate the dreamlike memory sequences (without the use of CGI), and much more.
excerpt_original: Can I go again? The writer-director discusses his latest, a screwball caper—with a touch of Baumbachian melancholy—about a regretful movie star played by George Clooney

article_text:
Films and events

Journey

Clarissa

Sophie Okonedo shines in Arie and Chuko Esiri’s (Eyimofe, LFF 2020) sophomore feature film, a delicate, sun-soaked re-imagining of Mrs Dalloway, set in contemporary Lagos.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Directors Arie Esiri, Chuko Esiri

Screenwriter Chuko Esiri

With Sophie Okonedo, David Oyelowo, India Amarteifio

Nigeria-USA 2026. 134min

Courtesy of NEON

Languages English, Nigerian Pidgin With some English subtitles

Introduction

It’s the day of Clarissa’s garden party. Just as she’s set to reunite with old friends, she finds herself reflecting on a summer that shaped the course of their lives. Virginia Woolf’s beloved novel is the jumping-off point for this rich and captivating look at class and gender in contemporary Nigerian society.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains flashing images.

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury and self-harm.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Dao

The new film by Alain Gomis is a formally inventive, politically attuned meditation on the enduring ties of the African diaspora, and the meaning of family and community.

The Last Day

Acclaimed visual artist Rachel Rose gives Mrs Dalloway a contemporary makeover in her arresting mood piece, starring Alicia Vikander and Victoria Pedretti.

Mouse

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo excel in this moving drama about facing up to life in the aftermath of a tragedy.

article_text:
Barbara Kopple completes her trilogy on labor rights with “Union Town.” Following screenings at Venice and Toronto, it’s now heading to Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , where Variety spoke to her about the film.

“ Union Town ” follows U.S. delivery and warehouse workers employed by UPS and Amazon, as well as app-based “deliveristas,” as they fight for a better future. “I guess I’ve always been drawn to stories about people fighting for dignity and fairness in their lives,” she says.

Kopple has won two Academy Awards for her docs “Harlan County U.S.A.,” about striking miners in Kentucky, and “American Dream,” about the 1985-1986 Hormel strike. The latter was shared with Arthur Cohn.

“When I made ‘Harlan County’ and then ‘American Dream,’ I spent many years with the coal miners and the meatpackers, and with their families. Those experiences shaped me as a filmmaker and as a person,” she adds.

“I learned so much about their courage, about what it takes for ordinary people to stand up to powerful institutions and how deeply these struggles affect entire communities. That’s what drew me back. We’re living through another important moment in labor history.”

After the pandemic, many delivery workers started to feel they were “disposable,” observes Kopple.

“They were risking their lives for others, and people didn’t understand that. They didn’t think about those who delivered their packages or worked in the warehouses. That’s one of the reasons for this film: so that people can see and feel who these workers are. And never, ever treat them as ‘disposable’ again.”

Ultimately, Kopple wanted to tell a “human story.”

“I like to dig deep and really get to know people. I really love and respect them. They are my heroes; they’re so courageous and passionate. But you don’t often get to know them,” she notes.

“Documentary filmmaking gives us a chance to spend time with people and their communities, see their lives up close and understand, in a way, the complexity of the world we’re living in.”

Sometimes, it doesn’t take long to establish trust with her protagonists.

“It doesn’t take long if they want to talk,” she says.

“I spend time with them so that audiences can feel what their experiences are like. I really think documentaries can create empathy.”

Some of the workers she’s interviewing are honest about their disappointment in the system, and also in the American Dream.

“[One of them], William, was a musician in his home country. I think he still plays, but this is as far as he can go right now until he’s able to become a naturalized citizen, which is very difficult under our current administration, if not impossible,” she says.

Many feel isolated. That is, until they start experiencing kinship with those who understand their situation only too well.

“There’s a scene when [longtime Teamster union organizer] Tony Rosario is with his children. He shows them that you can’t break a big stack of kindling, but you can break one piece of it. It’s his way of teaching them about solidarity and the importance of working together so that you’re never alone. That’s how you win.”

According to Kopple, documentary filmmakers already know this to be true.

“We’re not competitive with each other. We want each other to do well. If one of us succeeds, many of us will.”

She never wanted her film to be dark. After all, she’s not just depicting the struggles. In “Union Town,” Kopple also documents victories. In 2025, delivery platform DoorDash agreed to pay $17 million to settle claims that it used customer tips to subsidize the wages of its workers in New York.

“It’s actually very hopeful,” she says.

“Years later, people will be able to look back on this film and gain a better understanding of what happened. They can’t erase this history.”

“When we were in Venice, we brought in Amazon workers and the crowd stood up and cheered them on. Seeing them happy and excited, and seeing their worlds up on a screen, was emotional for all of us.”

Today, documentaries matter “more than ever.”

“They allow us to slow down and really listen to people whose voices are so often ignored. We’re living in a time when so much information is moving so quickly through social media and news cycles. It’s hard to understand the deeper human stories behind what’s happening. We want to make our films even more now that it’s so difficult.”

Produced by Cabin Creek Films, “Union Town” is being sold by Autlook Filmsales.

article_text:
Der ghanaische Künstler Ibrahim Mahama hat den Arnold-Bode-Preis der Stadt Kassel verliehen bekommen. 2017 war sein Werk prägend für die Documenta 14 in Kassel und Athen

Die Preisverleihung fand am gestrigen Donnerstag in Kassel statt. Die Laudatio auf Ibrahim Mahama hielt die künstlerische Leiterin der kommenden Documenta Sixteen Naomi Beckwith. Der Arnold-Bode-Preis, der nach dem Gründer der Weltkunstschau Documenta benannt wurde, ist mit 10.000 Euro dotiert. "Ibrahim Mahama steht für eine Kunst, die berührt, herausfordert und im Gedächtnis bleibt – und die zugleich unsere Sicht auf historische, politische und ökonomische Zusammenhänge vertiefen oder verändern kann. So verbinden seine Arbeiten künstlerische Kraft mit gesellschaftlicher Verantwortung", heißt es in der Begründung des Kasseler Magistrats, der die Auszeichnung auf Grundlage einer fachlichen Empfehlung des Kuratoriums des Preises vergibt.

Mahama, geboren 1987, schafft Installationen, die ästhetisch an den Minimalismus des 20. Jahrhunderts erinnern, arbeitet dabei aber mit Materialien, die dem Erbe des Kolonialismus in der Weltwirtschaft nachspüren. Auf der Documenta 14 in Athen nähte er zusammen mit dem Publikum riesige Stoffbahnen aus Jutesäcken, in denen Kaffee oder Kakao transportiert werden. Damit verhüllte er dann in Kassel die Gebäude der historischen Torwache in der Innenstadt.

Mahama gehört inzwischen zu den prominentesten Figuren der Gegenwartskunst. Das Magazin "ArtReview" setzte ihn im vergangenen Jahr auf Platz eins seiner "Power 100"-Liste . Derzeit ist eine große Schau des Künstlers in der Fondation Cartier in Paris zu sehen . Zum Arnold-Bode-Preis gehört auch eine Präsentation von Mahama im Kasseler Kunstverein , die noch bis Sonntag, 1. November, zu sehen ist.

editorial_title_zh: 艾未未推出宏大的全新澳大利亚作品：“90%的艺术都是垃圾。真正的艺术是对现有秩序的质问”

article_text:
“I t’s like a film set. Like it’s not real,” the bemused Uber driver says as we pass through a succession of silent rural villages washed with milky sunlight. He’s right: signs of human life are weirdly absent during our windy journey through the Alentejo. I’m making my way to Ai Weiwei’s secluded farm, nestled deep in the Portuguese countryside, where arguably the world’s best known living artist has quietly lived for the last six years.

When I arrive, I am ushered inside a vast cathedral of a building, a replica of Ai’s erstwhile, and controversially demolished , studio in Shanghai. The space is cavernous. It’s gridded by huge wooden columns and its dizzyingly high ceilings are webbed with beams. There is no artwork on the walls, nor are there any obvious signs of production or activity.

“People say, what is this building for? For what? Fuck that. Maybe it’s for nothing,” Ai tells me with a shrug. “It’s empty. And emptiness, people cannot accept.”

Ai has been busy filling other vacant spaces: I’m visiting him to chat about the unveiling of his latest work, Mushrooms, this year’s Neil Balnaves Tallawoladah Lawn Commission outside Sydney’s Museum of Contemporary Art. Characteristically epic, elliptical and urgent, this installation is 40 metres in length, and consists of 500 identical cast iron sculptures of combat helmets on an elevated platform. The title alludes to the visual rhyme between mushroom caps and the shape of the helmets – as well as the fungal associations with decay, death and the fragility of life, brutally exposed by armed conflict.

“Curiosity” and “boredom” generally shape Ai’s creativity, and the origins of this particular commission are “very simple”. In 2015, Ai began work on Human Flow , his documentary on the migrant crisis for which he and his team travelled to 23 countries. The process of producing this film led him to reflect more deeply on the causes of these perilous mass movements across the globe: war – or more specifically, the mechanics and munitions involved in contemporary warfare.

“I studied for two years to understand the military, arsenals, who designs bombs, and how they are used. Then, when Russia threatened Ukraine and Ukraine asked for help from Germany, the German chancellor offered them 5,000 helmets . I laughed,” Ai says. “I thought, wow, that’s interesting. So, at the beginning of the conflict, you can say Germany or Europe did not understand the nature of the war.”

Last year, Ai also visited Ukrainian soldiers on the frontline four times. He scrolls through his iPhone and shows me pictures and footage he took during his time there: Ai being taught how to use a rifle, the troops sporting uniforms he had embroidered with motifs of sunflowers. He plans to use these clips in an upcoming film.

But he is keen that I do not simply see these experiences and this background as research for the new MCA piece. “I never prepare my life so I can make an artwork – or create artwork for my life,” he says. Mushrooms was also shaped by its future home, “a beautiful location” that he has visited several times, with a dramatic view of the Sydney Opera House. That interested him too: “That building represents rational, peaceful enjoyment … but at the same time we have to re-announce that there are wars going on and peace is essential for any civilised society.”

His choice of words – “re-announce” – is striking. Throughout our conversation, over green tea, Ai seems despairing about a collective and cold amnesia about the parlous state of our geopolitics; if not amnesia, our deliberate refusal to truly engage with the doomed state of our world. “We cannot be blind, we cannot say I don’t know the situation,” he says. “You know the situation and you just pretend you don’t know it.” When speaking about the genocide in Gaza, he seems, too, deeply concerned about the lack of connectedness within modernity, our failure to understand that “if injustice happens to one person, it happens to the whole of humanity as well”. Much of his art, not least his trip to the battlefields of Kharkiv , seems an attempt to reestablish a connection and commitment to other human beings, however difficult and dangerous that might be.

Can art play some role in offering him hope about the future of humanity? No, he says, typically pugnacious and plain speaking: “Art today is very corrupted – 90% of what we see in most institutions, or in so-called artistic circles, I think is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order. Art is not about representing so-called beauty, but rather to question the existing judgment about everything in politics, in life, in personal relations, in individual judgment – but this kind of art is never encouraged. People want you to behave, want you to be a nice guy, pleasant, cheerful, enjoying your life. And so most work we see in the museums is very decorative and sentimental, rather than having any relations to human struggle and our reality.”

The Chinese word for mushroom is 蘑菇 or mógū, a term often associated with slowness, delay and dawdling. While our discussion regularly returned to Ai’s dissatisfaction with the tardy pace of societal and institutional progress, the conversation itself was leisurely. Despite describing himself as “the most interviewed human being” and claiming to have been interviewed “more than 1,000 times”, he is generous, fleetingly mischievous – and often startlingly wise. I’m curious, after Mushrooms, where his interests might take him next. But his existence is not so teleological: he has no “goals”.

“The only thing we should try to do,” he says, “is live a life which can naturally capture the light.”

Ai Weiwei’s Mushrooms is free to visit now on the Tallawoladah Lawn at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney

Ai Weiwei

The comparison to Hitler’s Germany, while understandably controversial, is made by a subject themselves. If they are banal, it is a modern, oddly familiar kind. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer released The Act of Killing , an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed. Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.", "links": [{"text": "The Act of Killing", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/jun/27/the-act-of-killing-review"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/11381e2e83b92b9a4e7f824a819c3173dcfecc67/0_135_3872_2323/master/3872.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A group of people sitting in a bright yellow room. article_text:
A re we still talking about the banality of evil? When that overworked phrase was first used by philosopher Hannah Arendt, it described the blank persona of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann. Now, in NAZA , anonymised members of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza. The comparison to Hitler’s Germany, while understandably controversial, is made by a subject themselves. If they are banal, it is a modern, oddly familiar kind. These are articulate, middle-class millennials. They say they are leftwing and non-racist. Put differently, they could be Guardian readers.

And yes, one remarks , they have been conducting a genocide.

The work of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is shattering. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer released The Act of Killing , an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed. Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.

Before that, documentary wild card Errol Morris made Standard Operating Procedure , interviewing US soldiers who abused Iraqis at the notorious Abu Ghraib jail. Edging into drama, you might even include Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest , where the commandant of Auschwitz lives happily with his wife and children. (Glazer is an executive producer of NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian.)

Questions gnaw through them all. To begin: who is it that commits crimes against humanity? The answer can feel inconclusive. NAZA is filled with Tel Aviv high-fliers, some citing as justification the horrific attacks of October 7. But the American troops of Standard Operating Procedure are ordinary grunts in the “war on terror”. Meanwhile, in The Act of Killing , ageing street thugs recreate their murders of trade unionists and teachers as the action movies they imagine them being. Flamboyance blooms in the abyss.

In every case, what we see won’t leave our heads, even as we flail for an adequate response. The late critic Roger Ebert famously called movies “ empathy machines ”. But these films short circuit the machinery. How can we empathise with people who seem to show no remorse?

For some, NAZA presents a bigger problem than that. The Israeli government has floated stripping Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, among other threats. But even for audiences far from the Middle East, the film is hard to deal with. We may feel anguished just as we are reminded how safe our anguish is. We might even think about that most unfriendly word: complicity.

But perpetrator cinema is about more than complicity. It is about the attempt to fathom the perpetrator. Discussing NAZA on the Jewish Currents podcast, Oppenheimer spoke to that task. “To understand a crime as a human activity, we have to look at the human beings who undertake that activity.”

Or do we understand mass murderers enough through what they do? In 2013, The Act of Killing also met pungent criticism. One influential figure in British documentary publicly called it a “snuff film”. (Oppenheimer next made The Look of Silence , about the victims.) And NAZA has faced pre-emptive criticism from Palestinians, including poet Mosab Abu Toha, arguing that the last three years in Gaza have already been documented by Gazans. “It’s all there,” he posted on social media. “So what will this film add?”

In this reading, NAZA is accused of privileging the perpetrator – giving literal voice to those for who the best platform, perhaps, would be a trial at the Hague. And yet another question is both obvious and uncomfortable. What’s in it for them anyway?

In this year’s documentary Killing Anna , former Syrian army officers were catfished into discussing civilian massacres by an academic posing as a loyalist of Bashar al-Assad. But most perpetrators are wholly aware they are being recorded. As such, we might expect a sobbing confessional. Not quite.

The torturers of Standard Operating Procedure came close now and then, but only amid a lot of evasion. As further ethical complication, they were also paid for their interviews. With The Act of Killing, though, Oppenheimer found a still more disturbing truth – his butchers were gleefully unrepentant. (They also believed that, as an American, he would approve of garrotting leftists.) And in NAZA, Yuval Abraham has said some of his interviewees spoke from “the opposite of shame”. That word complicity comes up again. Should a film-maker be doing this?

The thing is, though, lack of shame has a price. “War crimes are defined by the winners,” an Indonesian gangster says in The Act of Killing. “I’m a winner, so I can make my own definition.” In these films, that definition changes hands. Brilliantly, Oppenheimer did it by granting his subjects the freedom to reveal their nightmare psyches. In NAZA, journalism of the highest quality draws out a guilty plea with a seemingly howling lack of conscience.

Palestinian accounts of the assault on Gaza have been wrongly ignored. The response, to this Israeli version, of the Netanyahu government is telling. Aside from menacing the directors, a mimicking rebuttal , Naza: The Real Story was recently launched, desperately trying to reclaim control of the story.

And a director’s “complicity” is often indispensable. In 2017, the scalding Adriana’s Pact saw Chilean documentary maker Lissette Orozco interview her aunt, rumoured to have worked for the secret police of dictator Augusto Pinochet. When it turned out she had, the aunt’s berserk response to what she saw as a family betrayal was crucial to the story. Now the exposures of NAZA come from interviewees who would presumably never have talked to Abraham and Szor were they not Israeli too.

But more than that – the fact they are is also proof that Israelis can still say no to this Israel. Vital as they are elsewhere, the real power of these films is in the societies they portray. Official Indonesian history echoed the gangsters’ tales of bravely ridding the country of communists. Oppenheimer made the film available free there. Now NAZA confronts the belief that atrocities are only ever down to far-right “bad apples”. In perpetrator cinema, a common thread is directing us to unseen hierarchies – the politicians and generals whose lies to their own people are now laid bare.

Put like that, hope almost glimmers. Still. These films advise caution. Hollywood movies are delivery systems for catharsis. Here, it is elusive. Near the end of The Act of Killing, the most naggingly sympathetic of the subjects starts to retch, as if his body is trying to expel his own past. But nothing comes up. And now we watch NAZA, and know what has happened in Gaza still happens today.

No, what hope perpetrator cinema gives us is specific. Appearing with Oppenheimer on the Jewish Currents pod, Palestinian film-maker Rami Younis recalled meeting a giant of his country’s cinema, director Hany Abu-Assad, whose movies had been accused of humanising Israeli police. “What do you think happens when you keep demonising your enemy?” Abu-Assad said. “What happens to you ?”

Usually “humanising” implies a soft focus. But NAZA and The Act of Killing remind us being human involves being capable of evil. They also offer the chance to fight back. The perpetrator of genocide refuses to see their enemy as like themselves – to truly look at them. With perpetrator cinema, though, we can look hard at people with whom we would like to share nothing – and say we are both human, however monstrous that also makes us.
